Our study reveals that the entropic measure can indicate spatial coherence and, consequently, directional emissions. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the entropic measure effectively captures the coherence of emissions, even when emissions are bimodal or biased towards specific angles. Furthermore, we show that the entropic measure can be minimized by optimizing the microcavity design, further illustrating its utility in evaluating directional emissions.

We examine the interaction between a thermal atomic ensemble and a coherent light source to investigate the collective effect on photon statistics.  A method is presented that applies a linear transformation to convert the complex atomic dynamics into a straightforward products of individual influences, allowing for the calculation of output photon statistics in terms of these influences.  The complexity of the problem is thus significantly reduced, and it is demonstrated that the collective effect on photon statistics is influenced by the thermal state's temperature in an oscillatory manner.  It is also shown that it is possible to retrieve the statistical properties of a system governed by linear differential equations with time-invariant coefficients by varying the thermal state's temperature.  This includes systems that exhibit non-thermal behavior due to limited time exposure.  The proposed method is relevant to applications involving atomic reservoirs used in quantum feedback control and the analysis of output fields in thermal environments.

Offline transfer learning poses difficulties for methods due to the presence of multiple interacting agents, as sharing experiences becomes complicated when training from only positive data. Our proposed approach, APPLearn, overcomes these challenges for Offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) problems by focusing on sequences of actions that lead to desired outcomes. APPLearn leverages these positive trajectories through a sequence-level criticism mechanism that adapts the training process to enhance the efficiency of the learning process. By penalizing actions that weren't part of the learned sequences, the system is able to minimize the discrepancy between the trained models and historical positive experiences, resulting in better performance when testing the models on new situations.

Treatment planning and verification images used for cancer treatment are aligned with the patient's actual position during treatment using MV images, which are aligned with the treatment beams. Traditional alignment techniques are primarily feature-based methods that rely on matching distinct features in two images. The success of these techniques can be hindered by the low spatial resolution and noisy intensity variations found in MV images, which can cause them to differ significantly from planning phase CT scans. In this study, we investigate the application of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in aligning MV images with treatment plans, specifically with patients positioned upright and treated for thoracic spine tumors. Compared to conventional methods using matched filter algorithms, our CNN-based alignment technique showed a mean distance error of 1.3 centimeters, which is an improvement over the 2.6 centimeter error achieved with conventional methods. Additionally, our technique produced a mean rotation error of 2.1 degrees, which is substantially better than the 7.3 degrees obtained with conventional methods.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the apparent inconsistency between the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics and Einstein's own theory of special relativity. This experiment revolves around a single particle emerging from a source with two openings, represented as two rapidity switches in the $z$-axis. Einstein's hypothesis suggested that his own theory would prevent quantum mechanical probabilities from occurring, yet this prediction was confirmed by quantum field theory. Furthermore, this scenario can demonstrate the phenomenon of single-particle entanglement when we consider the particle's rapidity change in relation to its momentum. If we accept the Copenhagen interpretation, a measurement of the particle's momentum will instantly influence its rapidity change, regardless of the distance between the source and the point where the particle is measured. This effect holds true even if we consider a classical influence on the particle's behavior. As a result, we can leverage this scenario to investigate the relationship between single-particle entanglement and other phenomena that exhibit genuine nonlocality, such as entanglement and steering. Our analysis indicates that single-particle entanglement is sufficient to produce steering of another particle, and as a result, it is sufficient to generate the particle's rapidity change. Additionally, this scenario can also demonstrate the inequality introduced by Einstein in 1927, showing that the ratio of the standard deviation of the rapidity change to the expectation value of the rapidity change is limited to

The Internet of Vehicles has introduced new challenges to security and privacy concerns, given the interconnected and sensitive information nature of IOV. As a result, security and privacy preservation have become critical objectives for research in this area. Federated Learning has emerged as an innovative approach to safeguard the privacy of users while training machine learning models, but it has limitations in terms of scalability and efficiency. To address these concerns, a Blockchain-supported FL framework has been proposed by various researchers as a way to enhance security and privacy guarantees. This review survey provides a detailed examination of currently proposed Blockchain-supported FL frameworks for reducing privacy risks and enhancing security in IOV applications. It also outlines potential design considerations for research on privacy-preserving machine learning in IOV.

V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose extreme evolution over nearly three years has been closely observed.  V392 Persei, which rapidly transitioned from a powerful nova outburst to maximum brightness within 51 days, exhibited typical nova spectral characteristics and exhibited high-energy radiation patterns similar to those of the most energetic novae, with its gamma-ray spectrum peaking at incredibly high levels.  V392 Persei's post-outburst evolution was marked by significant variability, including both steady mass accumulation and irregular mass ejections that affected its surrounding environment.  In a surprising twist, a recent data set revealed a second, more powerful nova-like explosion, dubbed the "superoutburst," that significantly exceeded its initial outburst in both luminosity and duration.  This analysis provides the first detailed examination of a nova's interaction with its surrounding interstellar medium and offers valuable insights into its orbital period and mass loss estimates.  V392 Persei's highly unusual behavior suggests that it could be an exemplary model for the rare class of gamma-ray luminous novae that share its distinct characteristics.

In quantum computing, the ability to perform a specific operation indicates its controllability. Research has been done on controlling two-qubit interactions in model systems, but controlling the interactions of multiple qubits at once is a less explored area of study. This research focuses on understanding the distinguishability of multiple-qubit operations in the toric code model, using a four-qubit operation known as the Toffoli gate as an example. It is found that in some situations, controlling a single two-qubit interaction is enough to achieve the desired multi-qubit effect, but in other situations, controlling all two-qubit interactions is necessary. It is also shown that some multi-qubit operations can be achieved with less control than is required for the corresponding combination of single-qubit operations. A method is described based on a four-qubit interaction that can be used to assess the controllability of any multi-qubit operation in this class. It is found that in some situations, controlling a single two-qubit interaction is enough to achieve the desired multi-qubit effect, but in other situations, controlling all two-qubit interactions is necessary. It is interesting to note that in some circumstances, controlling all two-qubit interactions is not necessary to achieve a particular multi-qubit effect that can be described with a single-qubit effect.

A proposed precoder codebook feedback encoding technique replaces codebook entries with estimates derived from fitting a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) to a set of uplink pilot signals, reducing the feedback load significantly. We investigate the performance of this GMM-based codebook and provide practical guidelines for training and using GMMs in real-world applications, including the challenges posed by time-frequency dispersion and low signal strength in uplink pilot signals. Through simulations, we demonstrate that even with suboptimal GMMs, the four-dimensional feedback encoding technique can achieve a 30% reduction in feedback load compared to traditional methods, and that the challenges mentioned can result in a 5 dB loss in system performance. However, this loss can be mitigated by using more dimensional feedback encoding, which reduces the impact of spectral efficiency loss to 10%.

A type of two-dimensional Hofstadter model that maintains robust, stable, and robustly stable, isolated islands on an irregular surface through continuous tunneling has been found. This discovery enables the stable, persistent movement of particles at islands' edges, even in the presence of strong driving forces. A new class of surface flows, robust to all driving strengths, is realized by exploiting this stable structure. This robust flow surface is vulnerable to the slightest equilibration forces, which hinders its experimental realization. Despite this, our findings suggest that, even in the presence of tilting, a specific flow surface can persist, allowing the observation of this novel phenomenon in experiments involving tilted surfaces.

A new limit on the rate of change in mass for objects in general relativity's linearized regime has been established, based on vacuum solutions for linearized gravitational waves. This limit, expressed as $\dot{M}_2 < 2.8 \times 10^{-29} (1 + z) \rm{kg/s}$, applies to the rate of change in Bondi mass and has been found to be relevant for regions where scalar perturbations are not significant. Additionally, this limit has been shown to be more constraining than current or near-future observational limits, and is expected to impact the evolution of objects such as black holes and neutron stars.

We investigated the formation of binary black holes originated from the first stars in the universe using a model for population synthesis. Our analysis focused on nuclear star clusters found within major galaxies, and it considered three significant processes that influence the evolution of these binary systems: gravitational waves, supernova feedback, and pair instabilities caused by massive star mergers. A new feature of our model is its ability to simulate pair interactions during the merger of two massive stars, which results in the formation of a binary black hole with a more moderate mass distribution. According to our population synthesis model, approximately 5.10 x 10^-5 of these binary black holes produce gravitational waves with characteristics that are similar to GW150914. This number increases to 5.47 x 10^-5 (1 sigma confidence level) or 1.01 x 10^-4 (2 sigma confidence level) when considering the likelihood of such events occurring. Our study also predicts the ratio of nuclear star clusters' binary black hole formations to the total number of such formations to be 0.23 +/- 0.13 (1 sigma confidence level). If such binary black holes are associated with gamma-ray bursts, then our model suggests that up to 12% (3 sigma confidence level) of all gamma-ray bursts observed are caused by the merger of two massive stars.

The extensive data set produced by the Gamma-Ray Burst Early Warning System and its successor, GECAM, holds significant value for training and testing cutting-edge machine learning algorithms. However, due to the system's real-time operation, accessing the training and evaluation dataset is limited, as it does not allow for modifications that alter the original data. To overcome this constraint, a portable emulator has been developed to replicate the features of the BRIGHT dataset used for training and validation, enabling researchers to explore different scenarios and test the robustness of their models. The emulator, named PBE, successfully replicates the statistical properties of the dataset as evaluated by various metrics, including the distance between the empirical cumulative distribution function of the actual and simulated data, which shows an average error of less than 0.01. The portable emulator has the potential to enhance the performance of the Gamma-Ray Burst detection system by allowing it to be tested against a wide range of scenarios, thus detecting more bursts more efficiently.

This article is devoted to exploring the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA_p and its analogue VMOA_p. BMOA_p is a part of the family of F(p,q,s) spaces introduced by R. Zhao and serves as the M\"{o}bius invariant subspaces of the Dirichlet spaces D^p_{p-1}. Our study on BMOA_p focuses on the properties of its functions, providing necessary and sufficient conditions for the membership in BMOA_p. These conditions are expressed in terms of integral functionals involving the logarithmic mean, and our findings reveal that the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA_p are not closed. Furthermore, we establish that the closure of the unit ball in BMOA_p consists of functions with bounded logarithmic mean, and demonstrate that this closure is equal to the space VMOA_p. Our article also discusses the relationship between the maximum modulus of f and the logarithmic mean, establishing that |f'|_{L^1(log(1+|z|)^{-1})} \leq 2|f|_{\ast}. Additionally, we investigate the continuity of the integral operator T_f on BMOA_p, obtaining its continuity norm as |T_f|_{BMOA_p \to BMOA_p} = |f|_{\ast}.

Researchers examine the output of 13 high-impact physics journals from 1974 to 2020, citing the Influence Score method. This approach quantifies the extent to which citations to a work influence future research. The study calculates the average number of Influence Score units accumulated by papers published per year. This value remains relatively stable over time despite growing citation counts. The study also finds that the density of influential papers correlates with the overall knowledge base, as measured by citation counts. However, the correlation between influence scores and citation counts declines over time, indicating that the density of influential papers is not the sole driver of growing knowledge bases. A separate examination of mathematics, computer science, biology, and medicine fields reveals similar patterns. The study finds that the increasing disparity between influential papers and knowledge bases is linked to a declining rate of new, influential findings, as evidenced by the slowing growth of influence score counts. The study also finds that the majority of influential scores are concentrated among a small percentage of the most highly cited papers. The model proposes a new influence score distribution that captures the disparity between the rich and the poor in terms of citation counts. The proposed distribution outperforms the current state-of-the-art in modeling the influence score distribution in terms of log-likelihood.

This research paper suggests utilizing a hybrid technique that combines phase shifting and beamforming to enhance security at the physical layer in wireless communication systems using relay assistants. The proposed method's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations with OFDM and FTN-OFDM systems, showing significant improvements in data transfer rates and reduced error rates in scenarios with single and multiple attackers.

Two-dimensional systems bounded by waveguides provide a suitable platform for studying quantum electrodynamics in confined spaces. In this study, our theoretical model focuses on a tight-binding representation of waveguides and diagonalized mean-field dynamics of quantum emitters. It emerges that near an emitter a long, narrow waveguide resembles a one-dimensional channel, while broad connections to the emitter enable channel creation and, as a result, stable light storage. Furthermore, by incorporating multiple emitters, we discover that the electromagnetic mode becomes non-local and topological, allowing for stable light transport between emitters. This finding can be experimentally verified using photonic systems based on frozen beam distributions, and it paves the way for implementing non-local, topological operations with quantum emitters.

In the complex context of an urban traffic intersection with automated and human-driven vehicles, we explore an essential challenge: precisely forecasting the movements of human drivers to integrate their actions into the automated vehicles' navigation. To achieve this, we first analyze the underlying factors influencing human drivers' behavior near an intersection and develop a statistical model to accurately predict their actions. Next, we incorporate this prediction model into the automated vehicles' navigation system using Model Predictive Control, which optimizes their speed and trajectory to minimize journey time while ensuring safety. Through numerical testing and a real-world traffic scenario simulation, our approach proves capable of handling the uncertainty inherent in human drivers' behavior and effectively reduces journey time while preventing collisions.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based evaluation methods lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used in text rendering.
Our novel approach, TextWorldExpress, introduces a high-performance alternative to traditional FSA used in text games, delivering a substantial increase in processing speed of up to one million actions per second.
By leveraging this new system, we were able to create more than 150 text games at varying difficulty levels, featuring intricate stories and diverse settings, and showcase the platform's capabilities by conducting numerous agent testing scenarios.

Deep learning models like LSTM have seen significant adoption in video-based classification tasks due to their high accuracy, however their resource requirements and energy consumption present significant challenges for portable, real-time applications. To address this issue, this study proposes a new memory mechanism for LSTM that significantly reduces parameters and energy consumption while maintaining high classification performance, and this model was successfully implemented on a low-power FPGA. Furthermore, this research involves the design of a classification network where the LSTM model is integrated with a feature extraction module to improve identification rates for difficult video datasets. Through the use of a advanced tensor decomposition method such as Hierarchical Tucker, the number of required memory components was optimized, and this approach was found to yield a 50-fold reduction in memory resources required compared to traditional methods. This innovative design results in a 2.5x improvement in energy efficiency and enables the accurate identification of video contents with low energy consumption.

This study examines the use of data enrichment techniques in NLP tasks with restricted data. The high-quality training sets in NLP typically rely on labeled sources, but often lack diversity and quantity. On the other hand, abundant but poorly labeled resources are often discarded due to poor quality. The proposed method involves using these undervalued resources to enhance the training data via various techniques, including noise reduction, but often results in little to no performance gains. For example, using unlabeled sources to train models with similar structure, or utilizing poorly labeled sources to create training sets via importance weighting, but these techniques generally fail to surpass standard performance benchmarks. However, the findings suggest that applying these techniques to models trained with restricted data may yield better results compared to standard baselines, thus indicating the potential for data enrichment to enhance the performance of models trained with limited labeled data.

The 1920s Einstein's static model was later disproven, yet it still influences present theories. General Relativity was later developed, allowing for more flexible thinking. In the context of Computer Science, graph theory was transformed by the 1930s "Four Color Theorem." A celebrated conjecture in present-day Computer Science is the "Graph Minor Theorem." In physics-inspired Computer Science, "Universal Computation" concepts have been developed using natural languages similar to Poincaré's "Science should be simple." This study's basic aim is to explore the "Feeble Gravity" conjecture put forth by the first author, which connects Computer Science and physics. A crucial aspect of this conjecture is the "Charged Operator Conjecture," which this study's second author has shown to be incorrect by providing a counterexample. However, this counterexample leads to an interesting variation of the conjecture, known as "Weak Conjecture," which this study shows shares a crucial property with the original "Strong Conjecture," specifically in relation to the "Four Color Theorem." Additionally, this study presents a counterexample to the "Graph Minor Conjecture" and explores the "Weak Conjecture" through the "Optimal 4-Coloring Problem."

To scale quantum computations for realistic applications, it is essential to efficiently divide large systems into smaller, independently manageable regions. We introduce a method for converging the wave function across these regions and evolving the model space without overlap, overcoming imaginary time evolution constraints with the quantum Hamiltonian. This approach is demonstrated through applications to a Mott insulator to metallic transition using a Mott-Hubbard model with Mott gap sizes of 0.5 and 0.25, and Mott gap closure at 7.5 doping in the Mott-insulator-to-metal transition. Our results show that quantum simulations can be efficiently performed on quantum computers with a small number of qubits in comparison to full-wavefunction imaginary time evolution.

Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific composition series, we establish in this study that the dimension of its associated Hilbert polynomial space is determined by the dimension of the ring's fiber at a specific prime, specifically when that prime has a certain height. Additionally, we provide a condition for when that prime's fiber has a specific dimension, which can be applied to improve existing results on the ring's fiber, particularly in cases where the ring's dimension is greater than one. This condition also yields a new result regarding the ring's singular locus.

The success of renewable energy sources in the future power generation sector will heavily rely on supporting technologies, including dispatchable low-carbon resources and flexible services. As a crucial component of these support technologies, the procurement of supplementary services through economic mechanisms has not been well-explored in literature, particularly in regions with high penetrations of photovoltaics and wind power. This study develops a new method for procuring supplementary services, involving multiple producers and consumers of electricity, and assesses its effectiveness in efficient power systems production and revenue generation for service providers. Furthermore, we investigate how this method can be optimized with policy tools, such as clearing house mechanisms, to enhance the efficacy of service procurement, and investigate the potential of this approach in different geographical regions.

XG Dai, an Chinese mathematician, discovered an innovative approach to understanding the behavior of complex functions by breaking them down into prime factors. Building upon this discovery, Dai and his colleague Guo can now explain the underlying dynamics of complex functions through the study of prime decomposition. Their work has far-reaching implications, shedding new light on the behavior of complex functions, especially those defined on the complex plane.

To study non-resonant Higgs boson pair production at the LHC, a new approach based on the matrix element technique is proposed to distinguish it from background, specifically for the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel, even without an advanced detector upgrade. 

By utilizing the properties of the Higgs boson to effectively reduce the experimentally accessible phase space and integrate out less informative variables, the method enhances the available signal-to-background ratio. 

For 13 TeV LHC energy and 300/fb of integrated luminosity, this approach shows an improvement in background suppression, specifically for low-mass $\textrm{HH}$ systems, leading to a notable increase in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\tau\bar{\tau}$ signal efficiency to 5.8%,  a more efficient signal extraction by about 3.5 times with the same amount of data, and a corresponding increase in $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\gamma\gamma$ signal efficiency to 11.3%.

We investigate how precise $e^+e-\to Zh$ and $h\to \gamma\gamma$ studies can reveal multi-Higgs doublet models. To generate these processes, we employ an effective Lagrangian approach based on the Standard Model and consider up to three Higgs doublets. To obtain accurate results, we perform a high-precision analysis, taking into account radiative corrections. In contrast, our calculation for $e^+e-\to h+{\rm missing\,energy}$, resulting from heavy Higgs boson exchange, is kept simple. The most sensitive parameters in this context are the masses of heavy Higgs bosons and their mixings with the lightest Higgs boson. We outline two possible research paths: one focuses on $e^+e-\to Zh$ and $h\to \gamma\gamma$ with varying threshold energies, while the other explores $e^+e-\to Zh$ and $h\to \gamma\gamma$ with precise measurements in the sub-AB negative log(10) range. In the second path, we find that the ILC can readily discover multi-Higgs doublet models even if the lightest Higgs boson mass is 90 GeV.

Saturn's upper atmosphere is characterized by slow-moving circulation patterns,
formed by massive vortices that develop over the planet's polar regions as a
consequence of its extreme axial tilt.  While Earth's polar regions exhibit similar
circulation patterns, they are significantly influenced by the presence of solid
landmasses.  Observations taken by the Gemini solar instrument on the Saturn
Observatory for Tracing AtmOspheric and Interior electric field Variations (SOT)
onboard the ATLAS (Arase) satellite, revealed a previously unreported hexagonal
structure within Saturn's northern hemisphere's upper atmosphere during the onset
of summer.  This discovery was further supported by modeling a local condition
within the atmosphere that could produce the observed hexagonal shape.  The Earth
is the only other planet in our solar system with visible circulation patterns in
its upper atmosphere, allowing for potentially monitoring of its weather by looking
for changes in the stability of Saturn's famous hexagonal storm pattern.

This study examines the Schrödinger equation under conditions that vary by time and location, specifically within and outside a fixed, convex boundary in three-dimensional space. If the boundary is sufficiently far from the starting point, we demonstrate that a wave function initially concentrated on a small area will spread over time and occupy increasingly large areas within the boundary and beyond. This evidence supports a broader conjecture that a finite distance from the boundary can be traversed in a finite amount of time.

We provide a novel proof that certain varieties of a specific type, varieties defined by the intersection of polynomial equations with specific constraints, can be accurately described through a statistical approach even when some of the data are missing, provided that the data come from a random source. This type of variety is generally difficult to analyze analytically, but our method shows that it can be understood through an algebraic transformation alone. The challenge lies in overcoming obstacles due to the characteristics of the data, such as integer rounding errors, which depend on the specific variables used. Our approach involves developing a mathematical framework that takes into account all possible combinations of these variables. The success of our approach has implications for areas such as cryptography and coding theory.

The manner in which the surface of materials is terminated has significant implications for their physical properties. This concept is particularly crucial when studying the properties of electronic materials near their surfaces. We investigated the extent to which the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ is influenced by surface termination by employing soft X-ray photoemission spectroscopy, low-energy electron diffraction, and scanning tunneling microscopy. Our results demonstrate that oxygen-rich termination causes the metal-insulator transition temperature to decrease with greater accuracy, deviating less from bulk characteristics than other termination conditions do. Conversely, we found that oxygen-poor termination led to increased distances between V atoms in the surface layers and resulted in transition temperatures that dropped more significantly than in oxygen-rich termination. These findings provide valuable insights into the surface science behind V$_2$O$_3$ and may also implicatively suggest that certain electronic properties of layered metals are governed by similar mechanisms when considering bulk and surface phenomena.

Our study uncovers the quantum double dark-rogue waves, an initially finite and non-overlapping matter-wave state that, upon motion and interaction with a stationary and strong headwind, suddenly transitions to an over-lapping state at a critical point. We numerically analyze the long-term behavior of this wave and find a contrast to regular dark-rogue waves through the formation of two distinct gaps in the spectrum. We derive a scaling law to explain the rapid collapse of Bose-Einstein condensation in quantum double dark-rogue waves. Our analysis also reveals the importance of transverse motion in wave dynamics, leading to a prediction of wave localization through a critical parameter that is independent of initial amplitude.

We introduce a novel notion of polarization for set of graded collections $E=\bigoplus_{i\in \Lambda} E_i$ belonging to a abelian category $\mathcal{A}$. This categorical concept is based on the work of Hennion and Mazzanti who explored polarization properties in the context of finite-dimensional vector spaces. The introduction of the polarization morphism $\nabla:E\to E$ a key tool that enables the proof of a significant result. Specifically, if $E$ is finitely generated and self-dual under $\nabla$, it can be expressed as a product of simple modules $S_i^{\oplus m_i}$, with a specific duality character defined by the number $m_i$. The interplay between the category's structure and the polarization morphism also yields an interesting invariant, the polarization degree $\delta(E)$. This invariant provides insight into the category's properties, revealing the presence of simple self-dual objects and offering a upper bound on the number of isomorphism classes within $K(E)$.

This study examines adjusted measures on the full orthogonal group that is related to measures on symmetric matrices. Specifically, it analyzes the relationship between certain orbital integrals of these measures as the scalar field changes. The study's key findings include:
1) When the scalar field is non-Archimedean, the adjusted measures' orbital integrals are essentially invariant under a specific group of transformations.
2) When the scalar field is Archimedean, a similar invariance holds only approximately, leading to a link between the adjusted measures' orbital integrals and those of a comparable measure on the special linear group.
3) This study's approach also implies a useful relationship between the adjusted measures' orbital integrals and a specific sum of periodic orbital integrals. This connection is particularly evident in the non-Archimedean case.

Researchers are leveraging spectroscopy and resonant techniques to gain a deeper understanding of matter in nuclear scales, albeit this sensitivity comes at the cost of momentum conservation, imposing significant challenges. A novel approach, resonant x-ray diffusion spectroscopy, offers a potential solution for detecting nuclear scales through a combination of time, energy, and momentum measurements. This technique's effectiveness was demonstrated in a previous study using a highly transparent water sample, and it showed promise for using a 570 eV x-ray beam to illuminate a target. However, the same method failed to yield a signal when applied to a more opaque water sample, highlighting the significance of optical thickness in this process. Prototyping of a next-generation device using resonant x-ray diffusion spectroscopy has also been proposed, and the results suggest it could provide valuable insights into the nuclear scales of heavier elements like carbon, tin, and lead with sufficient sensitivity.

We investigate the stability of quantum error correction circuits based on practical quantum computing architectures, specifically focusing on the boundary properties of these circuits when subjected to decoherence processes. By drawing parallels with influential classical spin models, we are able to leverage their well-understood phase structures to gain insights into the quantum systems' stability. Using the quantum corresponding state principle, we can relate the boundary properties of the quantum systems to those of their classical counterparts, allowing us to determine the quantum systems' threshold values for fault tolerance. Conversely, this framework also enables us to investigate the geometric characteristics of these systems' failure regions, and we find that these features exhibit notable diversity, stemming from the interplay between classical fractal boundaries and the effects of continuous measurement-induced decoherence processes.

Recent theoretical predictions stating that group VI elemental monolayers can't be in the form of a honeycomb lattice structure have been disputed by new experimental findings. In this study, it's been found that incorporating oxygen into these monolayers, specifically tellurene, makes them dynamically stable and topologically non-trivial in the form of a honeycomb lattice. Oxygen functionalization brings about unique electrical properties, potentially turning tellurene into a large-gap 2D topological conductor by triggering a significant gap opening while maintaining the Dirac point on the Fermion surface. A key benefit of this model is that it could facilitate the realization of a topological quantum state with a large gap, making it less prone to other influences and more reliable in holding a non-trivial topology when a small amount of disorder is present. Additionally, this model displays potential for being experimentally realized due to the small amount of strain required. A large gap of about 0.36 eV opens up in this model, and it's predicted that the conductance at the Fermi level could be brought down to the order of 10^-2 (Ω.cm)^{-1} under normal conditions with the help of a simple reduction method that doesn't need complex functionalization. It's predicted that the oxygen functionalization could bring about notable optical and Raman spectroscopy changes that could serve as experimental signatures for this model. We employ a mixed finite element method for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous medium, using a spatially discrete hybrid approach. By solving a linear system, with a symmetric positive definite matrix, we can obtain an exact solution for the pressure field. The velocity field is then determined through the projection method. A conditionally stable bound, independent of friction, applies to the mesh size parameter, with an optimal value achievable. Numerical results are presented to demonstrate the method's effectiveness.

A spin switch is an essential element in spin-based electronics, allowing for the controlled redirection of spin current. This device can be achieved to some extent using the spin Hall effect, but its efficiency is limited due to the counterbalance of two opposing processes. An alternative method involves utilizing the inverse spin-galvanic effect, which can produce a significant output voltage. However, this approach requires the presence of light, making it less suitable for practical applications. A more promising approach is based on the combination of the anantosorbptive spin accumulation and the inverse spin-galvanic effect, which can generate a large output voltage in response to a change in the termination surface. This proposal suggests using a single layer of a helical magnetic material to accomplish this, either by switching the magnetic field or the adjacent surface. A key advantage of this design is the possibility of using a very small amount of spin accumulation, which could involve utilizing a superconducting film. The proposed switch based on a helical magnetic layer and a superconducting film on top of a metal surface with adjustable surface termination demonstrates high performance, producing a large output voltage in response to a change in the magnetic field. This suggests the feasibility of using a single layer of a helical magnetic material to control a large spin current. This breakthrough could have significant implications for the development of spin-based electronics.

The exhaustive evaluation of alternative models through Bayes factors is computationally intensive, necessitating the use of parallel processing techniques to optimize calculation time. This study explores the potential of distributing the calculations across multiple processors via a single master processor, leveraging OpenMP for efficiency. Three parallel approaches are examined: a simple specification of parallel regions, a hybrid method combining serial and parallel processing, and a complex multistep algorithm. The study assesses the performance of these strategies, considering factors such as memory constraints, data size, and the number of processors. The results indicate that the complex multistep algorithm yields the best outcomes, leading to a substantial decrease in calculation time with only minor increases in estimated uncertainty. This study provides insights for researchers planning to execute Bayes factor analyses across multiple processors.

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which is available for public use.

We investigate the properties of a negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond under elevated temperatures, using optical detection of magnetic resonance (ODMR).  By analyzing the ODMR frequency shift and resonance intensity modification as temperature increases, we gather valuable insights into the local environment of the defect site.  Our findings suggest the presence of nearby holes and the significance of electron spin exchange is confirmed through simulation, with the estimated variation of local temperatures being around 20 Kelvin.  This research provides a useful framework for using N-V centers in diamond as sensitive thermometers, and different diamond growth methods are compared based on the quality of the defects found.

The complex neural networks within cortical regions represent a critical aspect of the brain's overall functioning, ensuring optimal achievement of goals set by the higher brain areas. Despite being integral to the brain's operation, the intricacies of these networks have only begun to yield their secrets in recent studies. This paper delves into the fundamental principles thought to underpin the interneuronal network's behavior within the cortex, hypothesizing that selection and control can be achieved through the interaction of excitatory neurons competing for limited attention. By drawing from established models of brain function, we derived a mathematical framework that can be applied to capture the underlying mechanisms governing the behavior of cortical neural networks. This framework can simulate the brain's ability to solve intricate problems by distributing computational tasks across multiple regions, providing a solid foundation for further exploration into the brain's solution-finding mechanisms.

Using field-theoretic methods, researchers studied a spin model with three-fold symmetry, where the SU(3) representation was placed on each site of a triangular lattice. The model was an antiferromagnetic Heisenberg type, characterized by strong interactions that caused spin frustration. The study focused on N\'{e}el-type spin configurations and examined whether they could minimize energy through a sigma-model representation. The calculation revealed that the energy of these configurations could be represented as a sum of two terms: one that indicated the presence of Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions and another that showed Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions could be irrelevant when the SU(3) representation was large enough, thus not stabilizing the N\'{e}el order. The relevance of these interactions was found to depend on the size of the SU(3) representation and an exchange interaction constant, and researchers discovered that the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions could become irrelevant when the representation was sufficiently large, thus not stabilizing the N\'{e}el order. The implications of these findings on understanding N\'{e}el order in frustrated systems are discussed.

In this paper, we establish a basis-spline foundation for both atomic and electronic systems through a Hartree-Fock framework, utilizing B-splines of varying order. This basis-spline foundation can efficiently model a wide range of central potential shapes, from step potentials to Gaussian-type, giving us a unified framework for solving central problems. We demonstrate the accuracy of this method by comparing our results to traditional finite difference and Gaussian-type orbital approaches, showing that B-spline orders of 4-6 yield highly reliable Hartree-Fock energy values and electron density maps. Furthermore, we explore the potential of this method for modeling time-evolution through the time-dependent Hartree-Fock equation using the basis-spline foundation, and we provide initial numerical evidence of success with this approach.

The concept of synchronization in populations of oscillators has been extensively explored over the years. However, researchers have consistently found that a specific, explosive phenomenon of synchronization occurs - where oscillators transition from an unynchronized to a synchronized state rapidly. This study seeks to establish a universal standard for measuring this explosive synchronization phenomenon across diverse categories of phase oscillators. By analyzing various models, the researchers identified a critical metric that predicts the onset of explosive synchronization, which is directly proportional to the square of the population size. This discovery reveals that the time it takes to complete the transition is inversely proportional to the square of the population size. Additionally, the study finds that the amplitude of the exponential increase is influenced by the type of oscillators used. The findings of this study provide valuable insights for the study of explosive synchronization in populations of map oscillators.

We investigate a fundamental optimization problem to decompose a positive semi-definite matrix into the sum of low-rank matrices, specifically focusing on its critical properties as the rank increases. Through an analytical approach, we establish a crucial theorem regarding the local and global behavior of the optimization landscape for this problem. From a Riemannian perspective, we demonstrate that by incorporating a specific geometry, the landscape becomes convex within a particular region, allowing us to leverage this convexity to develop an efficient and minimality-guaranteed algorithm for this class of problems. We validate the theoretical guarantees of our algorithm through extensive numerical experiments, revealing that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

A graph's edge coloring can be described as a tinting process, where each edge is assigned a color based on specific criteria. In the case of a bipartite graph, this process is relatively straightforward, as different color patterns can be applied to the two distinct groups of nodes. However, when a bipartite graph is part of a larger cubic graph, the edge coloring process becomes more complex due to the potential connections between groups. A question has been raised regarding whether a specific configuration of a cubic graph can be edge colored using a particular color pattern, particularly one that has been shown to work for all minors of a graph, except one. After examining various combinations, our research provides a first example of a specific configuration of a cubic graph that cannot be edge colored using a particular color pattern, although it can be colored using a different pattern. This discovery also raises the question of whether there are infinite possible configurations of a specific type of graph that cannot be edge colored using a particular color pattern.

We provide an update to Flath's conjecture, offering a modern identity for the Dirichlet L-functions associated with quadratic characters using the method of partial sums. Additionally, our findings can be applied to demonstrate related identities for gamma functions and other L-functions.

High-energy particles with masses beyond 10^16 GeV face significant obstructions in our current understanding due to instability phenomena, which are likely caused by slow-roll inflation or primordial composite particles. If these particles exist, their presence could significantly impact particle physics observations, with a possible effect on CP symmetry, baryon asymmetry, and neutrino masses. Additionally, their interaction with light particles could lead to notable distortions in the cosmic microwave background, and their gravitational influence might be observable in large-scale structure surveys. Furthermore, if these particles have a very short de Broglie wavelength, their interaction with matter could lead to a suppression of particle production in certain channels, which could be confirmed through future particle colliders, especially in scenarios where there is a multi-TeV threshold in production.

Our study reveals that a swimming body with a rigid core and flexible tail, characterized by viscoelastic properties, can exhibit asymmetrical front-and-rear cross-sectional areas. We discovered that this asymmetry significantly affects the body's stability in different fluid environments. Our findings indicate that viscoelastic properties have a more substantial impact when the swimmer's cross-sectional area is uneven, particularly when the body is tilted to one side. This phenomenon is attributed to a counterbalancing effect of normal force and frictional force on the swimmer. Our research also shows that elastic forces can compensate for irregularities in the body's shape, thereby maintaining stability. We have derived a stability criterion that takes account of helical swimming velocity, viscoelastic properties, and the asymmetry of the body's cross-sectional area. Our study provides the basis for further exploration of biologically inspired swimmers that utilize viscoelastic materials.

We investigated how populations of firms, using different genetic algorithms to set output levels, eventually converge to the Nash Equilibrium in a Cournot game, as the population size increases. Our study shows that a specific type of algorithm, one that integrates a target-fitness method and leaky genetic mechanisms, is capable of reaching the NE more efficiently than other algorithms. Additionally, we found that in large populations, all algorithms including the less effective ones can establish and maintain the NE. Conversely, in smaller populations, the efficiency of the firms' genetic algorithms has a significant impact on coevolutionary learning, where some algorithms fail to establish the NE no matter how long the learning process continues.

The growing threat landscape in cybersecurity demands increased vigilance, 
wherein existing vulnerability information can be utilized to enhance knowledge 
and forecasting capabilities. Although security vulnerabilities are extensively 
documented on websites like NVD, the sheer volume of content poses a challenge, 
making it difficult to effectively utilize this information through traditional 
methods. A proposed approach involves using unstructured NVD website data to
leverage the power of deep learning to enhance a pre-existing security ontology.
This approach includes two phases: first, a deep learning model extracts relevant
information from NVD website data, and second, a rule-based approach is employed
to transform the extracted data into usable conceptual relationships.
These relationships are then utilized to enhance a security ontology in Microcosm.
Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method is capable of accurately
enhancing an existing security ontology, and subsequently, a related knowledge
base.
This approach offers a promising solution to address the large-scale, unstructured
nature of security knowledge databases.
The effectiveness of this approach is validated through a comparison with two
alternative methods, and the associated code is openly accessible for replication.

The Ising model fails to maintain balance with regards to the number of up and down spins when doped with finite percentages of active particles, specifically with regard to an asymmetric opinion formation process. However, it has been observed that the degree of imbalance can be affected by the ratio of Ising to voter agents. Notably, at a critical point, the system switches from an uneven to an balanced state. Through analysis of the order parameter and a relevant correlation function, it was found that the onset of imbalance is marked by a system-wide transition from a symmetrical to an asymmetrical state.

This study aims to analyze the spread of mosquito-borne viruses, specifically dengue, chikungunya, and Zika, through the aerial movement of infected mosquitoes, influenced by temperature and humidity levels. By creating mathematical models that account for the impact of temperature, humidity, and wind on the movement and survival of infected mosquitoes, we can determine the effectiveness of control measures such as mosquito population management, aiming to reduce the transmission of these viruses.

Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) with physical sciences holds tremendous potential to revolutionize data analysis. However, the traditional approach of relying on deterministic methods to derive answers is being disrupted by the incorporation of probabilistic models, which bring their own set of uncertainties. The term 'epistemic uncertainty' has been coined to describe this ambiguity originating from limitations of data, model imperfections, and sampling methods. The breadth of problems covered by this paper encompasses model parameters, observational data, and predictions, spanning various types of models including Gaussian processes, neural networks, and Monte Carlo methods. The paper introduces an expansive set of techniques, metrics, and benchmark problems to quantify uncertainty in scientific applications of AI. The evaluation criteria for methods to handle epistemic uncertainty emphasize their performance, computational efficiency, and sensitivity to key hyperparameters. The comprehensive assessment of 13 different techniques across 11 benchmark problems, tailored to the intersection of machine learning and physical sciences, provides a detailed landscape of the current state of the field. The research demonstrates that carefully chosen methods can yield significant improvements, up to factors of 10, in accuracy when compared to more straightforward approaches, such as maximum likelihood estimators. The study also reveals that a diverse set of techniques, including Monte Carlo and Bayesian methods, can offer a robust solution to the problem of uncertainty quantification, thereby facilitating the exploration of more complex applications at the intersection of machine learning and physical sciences.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish in this study that the symbolic and ordinary power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$ share the same equivalence for a specific subclass of weighted directed graphs. Moreover, the paper also identifies the ideal $I^{(n)}(G)$ and its symbolic power $I^{s_n}(G)$ for a broader category of weighted directed graphs, referred to as tree-directed graphs.

We've derived field theories in $O(N)$ symmetric quantum field theories, based on a specific class of random matrix ensembles. These matrix models have a well-defined limit as the size of the matrices grows infinitely large, allowing us to determine important parameters of the associated field theories. We've calculated the renormalized mass and coupling constant of the quantum field theories for all matrix ensembles listed in Table 1, and our results can be applied to both finite and infinite $N$. We've also verified that in the $N$ approaches, our results accurately match established quantum field theories. Additionally, we've obtained new finite $N$ corrections for the Susceptible quantum field theories, including results for the renormalized mass and coupling constant that can be used to make more precise comparisons with experimental data.

Convolutional neural networks are integral to various image-scanning technologies that rely on cameras and have application potential in surveillance systems. A recurring issue with these systems is the presence of hardware faults affecting the accuracy of images captured and subsequent inference outputs. While techniques such as input preprocessing and artificial fault injection have been explored to counter these defects, there is currently no universally accepted method to tackle this problem across different scenarios. We propose a novel framework called Activation Interval Supervision (AIS) that targets the mitigation of hardware faults in convolutional neural networks by leveraging analysis of output activation patterns across neighboring neurons within the same layer. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through the conduct of artificial fault experiments on a benchmark dataset, and its advantages over competing techniques are verified through performance metric comparisons.

The algorithm we propose determines the apportionment of losses among companies in the event of a default, utilizing the European Banking Authority's method of calculating credit default risk. Specifically, we apply this algorithm to settle obligations with the Romanian Ministry of Finance, drawing on actual data, but the scope of the study can be expanded to encompass more comprehensive scenarios.

This study establishes a one-parameter group of transformations based on the Jordanian twist, deriving its associated differential equation. By converting the problem into a matrix form, we can determine the explicit form of the one-parameter group of transformations. This, in turn, enables us to derive a precise formula for the n-fold extended Jordanian twist.

Constructing a shared semantic space across multiple languages is the foundation for successful cross-lingual studies, including translation, text mining, and image analysis. Current approaches primarily employ neural network methods for word representations that learn from monolingual data and then map words of different languages to a common space. These techniques generally rely on multilingual corpora containing annotated information for multiple languages, which is scarce in reality. Additionally, the representations learned from these methods often have difficulty capturing the underlying structure of a language. In response to these challenges, we propose learning a shared semantic space that is consistent with intrinsic language structures by leveraging only monolingual resources, specifically by utilizing pre-existing clustering information available for each language. Our evaluations demonstrate that incorporating this clustering information enhances the quality of cross-lingual representations, and our method outperforms the competition in multiple tests. Moreover, our approach proves particularly beneficial for smaller languages.

The study reports the initial measurement of midrapidity production of pions, kaons, proton and phi mesons in Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV. Various observables including mean particle charge, mean number of particles, particle yield ratios and the expansion velocity of the medium at early time have been calculated and compared to the CLAS collaboration's data from 11 GeV proton-proton collisions, LHC data at 2.76 and 5.02 TeV, as well as the model known as iEBE-VISHNU.

The MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset has significantly accelerated the study of dialogue state tracking, yet contains considerable annotation flaws that significantly impede the robustness of models in real-world applications. The recent releases of refined datasets, MultiWOZ 2.1 to 2.4, are not entirely label-free from errors. The current challenge lies in developing a method that is insensitive to these annotation imperfections. In response, we propose a novel approach, named Inferred-Self-CorrecTion State tracker, or ASSIST for short, tailored to address this issue. The ASSIST tracker initializes the dialogue state based on user inputs and refines it through self-correction using the speaker's response. The speaker's role is inferred from the dataset, enabling the state to be updated. The proposed tracker is capable of handling diverse and potentially misleading responses from the speaker. The ASSIST tracker achieves a high overall success rate of 73.19% in matching the gold standards of MultiWOZ 2.1, outperforming existing methods while exhibiting a notable gain of 5.19% over the state-of-the-art method, showcasing its effectiveness in handling real-world dialogue state tracking scenarios.

In late October 2019, widespread protests erupted in Chile, centered on Santiago, spreading rapidly to 18 regions and ultimately affecting every commune in the country. Using epidemiological methods, we developed a simulation model to explain the protests' spatial and temporal patterns. The model accounts for non-local connections between communes based on Chile's road network and identifies key areas that drove the spread of protests. Analyzing the model's results in conjunction with real-world data, we found that the simulation accurately captures the observed peak activation patterns across all communes. Furthermore, the model reveals specific critical periods that influenced the protests' outcome, and we explore the potential policy interventions derived from its findings. The challenge of modeling complex social phenomena using mathematical methods is addressed, and the role of collaboration between mathematicians and social scientists in developing applicable theories is discussed. The model and its analysis also provide a framework for evaluating the efficacy of response measures, such as lockdowns, and can be adapted to facilitate dialogue between government officials, civil leaders, and the broader community.

By analyzing a sample of 65 galaxies at a distant epoch, we examine the correlation between star formation rates (SFRs) estimated from spectral energy distribution fitting and those inferred from optical spectra in the Brackett-gamma (Br gamma) line. Although previous studies have established a link between Br gamma and ultraviolet to near-infrared SFR estimators, our research aims to explore this connection further by comparing Br gamma-based rates to those predicted by the SED fitting technique. By examining potential biases and scatter in their relationship, we investigate how Br gamma might be used as a standard for validating SFRs obtained from SED fitting. Our analysis suggests that Br gamma-based rates tend to be overestimated by about 0.5 dex when compared to predicted rates, and show a significant scatter of 0.8 dex. This relationship may be influenced by the selection of SED models, as well as Br gamma-based rates. If this connection holds for more recent studies, our analysis suggests that Br gamma-based rates will be generally consistent with predicted rates once the biases associated with our study are accounted for.

We are studying a critical boundary that involves breaking down real polynomials into the sum of squares and determining the nature of the positive semi-definite matrix. Specifically, we are examining the set of strictly positive semi-definite matrices, defined as the intersection of the sum of squares cone and the set of positive semi-definite matrices with non-negative diagonal entries. Our research focuses on understanding the geometric and algebraic properties of this complex high-dimensional space. We are looking at methods to identify whether a given set of linear functions can be used to determine the optimal value of a semi-definite program when restricted to this boundary compared to the entire positive semi-definite matrix cone. Our findings show that such a set of linear functions does exist and can be found by solving a linear program, although it may not be unique. Our approach also enables us to establish that there are infinitely many optimal solutions for achieving the minimum value when restricted to the strictly positive semi-definite matrix. Our results can be seen as a special case of a more general theorem that addresses the infinite complexity of determining the optimal value of a semi-definite program when the matrix has a specific boundary property.

In high-energy experiments, a particular type of neutrino interaction known as semi-hadronic or semi-leptonic can provide significant background in various searches or conceal a crucial process in certain phenomena. To better understand these reactions, we need to reevaluate the system of neutrinos and their counterparts by considering multiple variables, including massive particles that participate in reactions and contribute to a fundamental process, as well as the energy at which the process occurs, which in this case is extremely high, typically in the range of 100 to 1000 GeV, and above 10 GeV for the neutrino system. 

We have established a set of general constraints on a set of neutrino mixing parameters that are based on a combination of experimental data and a comprehensive review of the theoretical principles that govern neutrino interactions, which can be expressed in terms of a fundamental theory known as perturbative standard model or its extensions.

In addition, we have conducted an in-depth analysis of the detection capabilities of a variety of neutrino experiments that involve lepton detection and participated in the review of the neutrino diffusion process in a medium that involves at least two particles, which enabled us to develop an accurate description of the system's properties, which we used to estimate the detection capabilities of the experiments, which in turn enabled us to establish upper limits on the rates at which neutrinos participate in semi-hadronic processes that involve at least two particles.
