Previous research has established a new approach to studying turbulence within galaxy clusters through X-ray observations, specifically by analyzing the structure functions of temperature fluctuations. However, the accuracy of these measurements has not been thoroughly assessed, particularly in terms of potential biases and uncertainties. This paper investigates the inaccuracies inherent in measuring temperature fluctuations and their associated uncertainties, which stem from instrumental and physical sources. It also examines how these inaccuracies affect the estimation of structure functions and associated scaling laws. By understanding and quantifying these measurement flaws, this study aims to lay the groundwork for a rigorous statistical analysis of the data presented in a companion paper.

We define an upper rich Ramsey property for graphs in relation to a specific set of colors. It's shown that in the context of graphs containing a specific edge configuration, namely triangles, a particular group of vertices will exhibit upper rich Ramsey behavior for certain colorings. Additionally, upper rich Ramsey properties are found to apply to the vertices within specific subgraphs, specifically those formed by the edges connecting two highly connected components in an infinite graph.

Located within the center of the Milky Way lies the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a ring-like structure composed of molecular gas that is closely tied to the galaxy's black hole. Studies have shown that the mass distribution within the CMZ is unevenly structured, following a diagonal orientation that reflects the path of the galaxy's circular motion. To better understand the geometric relationship between the mass distribution and the orbiting gas in the CMZ, we developed a statistical method to analyze the two-dimensional correlation of objects in the region. By applying this method to a comprehensive molecular line survey, we obtained a detailed view of the anisotropic mass configuration that influences the motion of gas in the CMZ. Our results suggest that the mass distribution in the CMZ is skewed, with a longer semi-axis aligned with the diagonal pattern, and a smaller, perpendicular semi-axis. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that the anisotropic mass configuration in the CMZ is consistent with a elliptical shape that is tilted at an approximately 45-degree angle. This finding has implications for our understanding of how the mass distribution in the CMZ affects the motion of gas in the region, and our method can be applied to other studies of mass distribution in circular orbits.

A potentially life-threatening condition called bilateral facial paralysis, also known as Bell's palsy, requires prompt medical attention within 72 hours of its onset to minimize the risk of long-term complications. This paper presents a groundbreaking approach that utilizes machine learning to automate the detection of this condition from video recordings of a person's facial expressions. Our system specializes in identifying the early signs of Bell's palsy by analyzing a person's eye movements and the surrounding facial area. In particular, it extracts key frames from video clips and trains a neural network to detect the presence of the disease based on these frames. Our experiments demonstrate that this technology is capable of detecting Bell's palsy with high accuracy (94%) on a large dataset consisting of 800 video clips, along with additional datasets comprising 2000 images and 600 video clips. Moreover, this technology has been successfully demonstrated at the IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV) 2019 in Seoul, South Korea, as part of a technology showcase.

The Quantum Double Quantum Computer is capable of executing quantum circuits from lattice gauge theories, offering a promising avenue for the study of quantum field theory using quantum simulation. In this paper, we explore the application of this system to the symmetric phase of quantum electrodynamics by utilizing qutrits to enhance the simulation of the electromagnetic field. We provide an expanded quantum circuit for the qutrits, detailing a quantum simulation that involves interacting finitely with matter fields on a spatial lattice while maintaining the freedom of massless photons. This paradigm includes an improved photoelectric effect and enables the creation of quantum states of electromagnetic fields via electromagnetic reactions. Furthermore, in the context of quantum simulation, we examine the photoelectric effect in relation to the reaction of an electron with qutrit mass and observe the emergence of continuous sound modes within the quantum simulation, closely resembling those of the electromagnetic field's infinite-depth, continuous mode spectrum.

The interplay between intense lasers and highly polarized positron sources could potentially lead to significantly increased positron polarization. We investigate the interaction between a linearly polarized laser and a water-ice target, specifically looking at how it affects positron polarization in the quantum electrodynamics limit. Using macroscopic positron polarization calculations and taking into account the effects of thermal motion in the target, we find that, with appropriate polarization of the target itself, the positron polarization can be increased by more than fivefold, reaching greater than 90% in some cases, and that this increase can hold through to densities where the density of electrons is nearly equal to that of photons. Furthermore, we find that the optimal polarization of the target can increase the positron polarization to greater than 99%.

A group G is considered a long-distance group if there is an infinite number of points at a minimum distance from its core, which is comprised of a finite number of elements. This concept can be applied to any group, including finite groups, and we explore the criterion for a finite group's large diameter property. Specifically, we establish that a finite group's large diameter property is equivalent to the number of double cosets being infinite, which simplifies a previous condition obtained by Bachman, Katz, Katz, and Shalev. Additionally, we derive a more straightforward condition for the large diameter property, which is that its diameter is greater than its core's size.

This research develops a temperature sensing technology that utilizes a CMOS temperature detector, allowing for accurate temperature readings and triggering of thermal shutdown mechanisms. By integrating this detector into various systems, even those utilizing low-power designs, it is possible to monitor temperatures across different frequencies and voltage ranges. This enables more effective prevention of overheating in integrated circuits. Furthermore, this temperature sensing technology is highly versatile, making it suitable for application across both mobile and data center settings. Building upon previous work, this research refines the design of the temperature detector in [1] by modifying the biasing circuit to utilize a p-channel MOSFET, achieving a more compact design with improved temperature sensitivity. The modified design exhibits a more precise temperature reading with an error of less than 1.5 degrees Celsius and a conversion energy of 1.46 nanojoules. However, this research encounters an unexpected challenge while transitioning to a 28nm process node. The cause of this difficulty is investigated and a novel approach is proposed to resolve the issue. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the feasibility of integrating the temperature detector into a test chip, providing a precise temperature reading with an error of less than 1.4 degrees Celsius and a conversion energy of 1.06 nanojoules.

The hypothesis that stars possess rigidly connected magnetic fields and rotation is widely used in analytical and numerical models. However, the long-term stability of such configurations in stars has not been thoroughly determined. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of highly symmetric magnetic field stability in rotating stars, focusing on nonlinear processes influenced by the interaction between magnetic field and gravity forces. Our study reveals that in stars with convective cores, where heat is transported by convection, magnetic field instability can be mitigated by the convective core itself. In stars without convective cores, where heat is radiative, the stability is determined by the nonlinear interaction of unstable modes. This can sometimes lead to the formation of magnetic field configurations that are themselves unstable, potentially resulting in magnetic field distortions and associated effects on the star's behavior and properties. This understanding has implications for the search for pulsar stars, as well as the study of magnetized white dwarfs and neutron stars.

Using the functional renormalization group (FRG), our study calculates precise fluid dynamics for the $O(N)$ model in zero-dimensional quantum field theory by solving a set of partial differential equations derived from the FRG approach. We verify the renormalization group flow equations for the $O(N)$ model in zero-dimensional quantum field theory, solving them analytically for both the Schwartz model and the $\phi^3$ theory. We validate the renormalization group flow equations for the $\phi^4$ theory through numerical methods. For all cases, our findings match established results obtained through other methods, providing a crucial check for the validity of our approach. Additionally, this work paves the way for extending the FRG method to more complex scenarios, including field theories in higher dimensions and near phase transition thresholds.

Music notation symbols convey both pitch and rhythm, yet are not a linear representation of either. Existing neural models for music have primarily drawn from graph neural networks and transformer models, often using separate inputs for pitch and rhythm information. This new approach uses a unique, unified input representation, leveraging a form of self-supervised attention called meta-inquiry, to process both elements of the notation. When applied to the task of improving reading abilities, tests on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, surpassing current state-of-the-art techniques.

Building on the concept of Lie groupoids providing a geometric framework, we establish a comparable framework based on smooth stacks. This stack-based framework is shown to be equivalent to the Lie groupoid framework, establishing a bridge between these two distinct geometric frameworks. Furthermore, a connection between the stack-based framework and the approach using differential geometry on manifolds is demonstrated, proving that a stack-based framework applied to ordinary manifolds yields the standard geometric framework.

A distinctive infrared dark filament, referred to as the Dragon infrared dark filament, has been the subject of analysis in order to gain insight into the core formation process within it. Observations from the Submillimeter Array and the Atacama Large Millimeter/band Imaging Experiment reveal a protostar and an associated 1.3 mm continuum density gradient that is highly aligned with the filament's axis. In addition, observations from the Spitzer and the Infrared Astronomical Satellite uncover a submillimeter dust temperature gradient that mirrors the density gradient's behavior. The Dragon infrared dark filament exhibits a critical density threshold where star formation is observed to occur, suggesting that it has reached a critical stage in its evolution. The Dragon infrared dark filament is found to have a mass ratio that is similar to that of the Taurus B1 core, indicating that it is in an early stage of evolution. In contrast to the Taurus B1 core, which has already given birth to a massive star, the Dragon infrared dark filament is characterized by its absence of massive star formation, instead featuring low-mass stars. The time it takes for the Dragon infrared dark filament to reach this stage of evolution is estimated to be around 2.5 million years, and it is expected that it will produce a massive star in the near future.

This study explores the underlying algebraic and relational structures for Godel modal logic and its extended varieties, such as classical propositional logic based on prelinearity and its combinations with distributivity and its application to systems of modal logic.

LiDAR systems are widely utilized for safe and efficient road network mapping by automating the collection of 3D point data. These datasets contain numerous critical information points, including road markings, curbs, and operational intersections, which are essential for advanced driver-assistance systems and autonomous vehicle navigation. Although significant progress has been made in leveraging LiDAR data for spatial awareness, there is still a significant challenge in beign able to extract relevant information from these 3D point sets to support CCAV systems. With the emergence of new 3D feature learning techniques, it is now possible to extract contextual and hierarchical 3D descriptors from LiDAR data, but it remains to be seen whether these methods can effectively tackle the practitioners' problems of extracting critical information from these datasets. With the high costs associated with collecting and labeling large LiDAR datasets, it is also unclear whether existing methods can be robust to variations in LiDAR data when tested on smaller datasets. This work aims to address these uncertainties by evaluating the current state-of-the-art 3D LiDAR learning techniques on a newly collected and extensively annotated dataset containing critical information points, and also testing their performance under real-world LiDAR data collection conditions. With the future direction of LiDAR-based 3D learning towards extracting information from these datasets becoming increasingly dependent on the outcomes of this research, it is essential to share the findings with the community. We analyze a set of random variables defined by conditionally exponential distributions, located on the sphere in three-dimensional space, with the position of one variable depending on the values of the others. By examining this single layer of variables, we derive a precise formula for their joint moment of any order, achieving this by differentiating the corresponding probability density function. As a result, we obtain formulas for the raw and central moments of these variables. Additionally, we show that when the sphere's center is shifted, the corresponding shift formula applies. This finding has implications for research areas including harmonic analysis on the sphere and stochastic geometry.

The observation of extremely energetic cosmic particles poses a mystery in physics. To further investigate this phenomenon, researchers are looking for connections between high-energy cosmic rays and neutrinos. To explore these connections, this study focuses on linking sources of neutrinos with ultra-high-energy cosmic rays, specifically probing for spatial correlations between neutrino and UHECR populations. By analyzing a large dataset of neutrino and UHECR events, this study examines the spatial distribution of UHECR events surrounding neutrino sources, restricting the search to sources emitting multiple neutrinos, which are more likely to have a genuine origin. The analysis reveals that UHECR events are clustered around these sources with an excess density of approximately 8.1+2.5-2.2, observed at a 4.6-sigma confidence level. Furthermore, when considering only sources with more than one neutrino detected, the analysis finds an excess density of 13.3+5.8-4.1, correlated at a 3.3-sigma confidence level.

The interplay between surface tension and viscosity in foams gives rise to unique properties that affect friction on both flat and textured surfaces. Research has previously focused on the long-term behavior of foams in response to external forces, but there is a lack of understanding regarding the influence of surface geometry on viscous liquids at high shear rates. This study investigates the dynamic interaction between a liquid foam and various textured surfaces across a wide range of velocities, discovering that the key factor determining friction is not the type of liquid, but rather the shear rate at which it is measured. Additionally, it was found that higher texture heights lead to increased static friction, but also result in reduced kinetic friction due to the creation of channels that allow foams to flow more easily. This counterintuitive phenomenon, which we term "texture-induced friction," provides insight that could also be applied to other non-Newtonian liquids.

This study employs a unique combination of deep learning and entropy to differentiate normal skin tissue samples from carcinoma samples using the HE staining images of human skin tissues. The proposed method consists of two components: first, a deep learning algorithm called IncPAN based on incision points, and then an entropy-based thresholding method. The IncPAN algorithm leverages residual learning and efficient skip connections to accurately define the boundaries between cancerous cells, whereas the entropy method serves as a secondary validator to eliminate anomalies by measuring the diversity of cell arrangements. A consortium of seven experts in cell image analysis pathology reviewed and validated the results, achieving an outstanding 97.76% accuracy rate in classifying carcinoma samples. Furthermore, the proposed method demonstrated exceptional robustness in identifying outlier samples, prioritizing images with more diverse cell arrangements for further pathological examination.

The interplay between surface tension and rotation in a suspended layer over an increasingly permeable substrate reveals a critical point at moderate rotation speeds, characterized by a sudden and persistent shift from orderly patterns to chaotic ones. The normally stable fingers that form in this context can suddenly shift to an unstable configuration, with multiple narrow bands forming in the process. This degree of flexibility is unique to this specific combination of forces and constraints, making it an intriguing phenomenon that sets this particular system of fluids apart.

Building on a new theoretical concept, we recast the microscopic dynamics of phase space for an N-body system through Hamiltonian evolution. This approach is unique because it eradicates the inherent bias caused by constantly changing volume in phase space. We explored this idea in the context of a expanding expansion where a group of harmonic oscillators expand freely. Utilizing this framework, we derived an observable law that deviates from the typical prediction of a scaling theory. The discrepancy arises due to the intricate interplay of mutual correlations among the particles, resulting in an irregular distribution of phase space. Specifically, we found that the phase space volume varies according to a non-universal law that differs from $V_N^\gamma$ where $\gamma$ is a constant. Instead, we discovered that the expansion follows a more complex path which we define as $\Omega_N$. Moreover, our theory offers a pathway to identify Hamiltonian paths that satisfy $\Omega_N$, thereby providing a new route for exploring the dynamics of expanding systems.

Scientists have identified numerous ethynyl derivatives of aromatic compounds, such as benzene and its six-membered ring analogues, cyclopentadiene and cyclopentatriene, emanating from the TMC-1 molecular cloud using radio astronomy. A study of these compounds, specifically ethynyl cyclopentadiene and its isomer ethynyl cyclopentatriene, revealed their abundance and how they were created through chemical reactions. The study found that cyclopentadiene and its derivative prevail over cyclopentatriene and its counterpart, with a ratio of approximately 5:1. The researchers also established a method to calculate the total abundance of these compounds in the cloud, finding it to be around 3.5 times higher than the abundance of cyano cyclopentadiene.

The look-forward attention mechanism in neural machine translation has been widely applied due to its computational efficiency. However, research indicates that it can result in a source-target ordering effect, leading to suboptimal translation choices. We propose a novel, bidirectional attention mechanism that selects relevant source sentences to combine with the target sentence, thereby overcoming this ordering constraint. This approach enables the model to focus on both source and target order, thus potentially producing more natural word orders and improving overall translation quality.

The advent of cloud computing has superseded grid computing, yet understanding is lacking about the historical context in which cloud computing emerged. A prominent IT paradigm, involving applications with high informational demands, remained elusive to developers until the advent of cloud computing. The absence of clear documentation and the retirement of key figures have obscured the development processes of grid computing. This study involves interviews with influential developers to uncover the creative processes that led to the development of grid computing, revealing that a translation framework played a pivotal role in shaping its development and ultimately laying the groundwork for cloud computing. Furthermore, it became apparent that developers applied lessons learned from this experience when creating cloud computing, leveraging similar techniques such as mapping and federating to tackle complex challenges. This study offers valuable insights into the precursor to cloud computing and the underlying principles that it shares with cloud computing.

We've developed a new theoretical model that incorporates a dark fluid with dissipative properties within the framework of the Einstein Field Equations. This model is an innovative variation of the General Relativity theory, particularly in the universe's late stages. The Einstein Field Equations have been modified to accommodate a dissipative dark fluid, which is represented by a set of nonlinear and hyperbolic conservation laws. The conversion rate of dark matter to dark energy is influenced by an acceleration field that originates from a scalar field, thus offering an explanation for the universe's present-day dark energy dominance. Unlike conventional reversible dark fluid models, this new approach provides a more realistic framework that aligns with the principles of irreversible thermodynamics. As a result, we've derived a set of differential equations describing the universe's evolution, which incorporates a non-zero entropy generation term. The universe's evolution equations, along with the initial conditions based on the Big Bang cosmology, are solved using numerical methods, thus providing a more accurate representation of the universe's evolution due to its irreversible nature.

Students' curiosity is seen as a vital factor in promoting successful learning, but there's a lack of research on what sparks curiosity in group learning settings. To address this knowledge gap, we developed a novel theoretical framework focusing on the interpersonal components of curiosity. Utilizing combined video and audio data from observations of small groups, we developed new metrics to measure curiosity levels and analyze their connections to other behavioral aspects. Our empirical results revealed intriguing connections between curiosity, task engagement, and conflict within the group, indicating future directions for research and potential applications in creating data-driven insights from observational studies.

As spatially indexed data sets grow, Gaussian processes become less feasible to compute due to their O(n^2) complexity, leading to the adoption of alternative methods for modeling and inference. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a novel, scalable approach based on Mat\'ern Gaussian process models, compatible with graph structures, and demonstrates its effectiveness through computational complexity reductions, including O(n) expectations and O(n) linear operators, facilitating applications in vast data sets. Additionally, this paper showcases the effectiveness of these models through synthetic and real-world experiments, such as predictive reconstruction, signal recovery, and remote sensing.

The precise detection of urban road structures is crucial for developing advanced navigation technologies and efficient urban planning methods. However, the traditional approach of using laser sensors and GPS has significant costs associated with it. A novel method is proposed to locally optimize the positioning of ridesharing vehicles within a city to effectively map its road systems by collecting GPS data. The problem of road detection is formulated as a nonconvex optimization problem that aims to minimize the cost of vehicle trips while maximizing the coverage of unknown road segments. A convergent algorithm is developed to solve this problem, and its performance is evaluated using simulated data as well as actual GPS recordings from a large number of ridesharing vehicles in a medium-sized city. The proposed method demonstrates the ability to detect urban road systems at a lower cost compared to a random vehicle trip approach, and the results highlight the importance of considering the implicit data provided by GPS in optimization problems.

Our research investigates the significance of neutrino and dark energy sector contributions to the invisible decays of the $J/\psi$ meson, specifically for the process $J/\psi\to \gamma + \text{invisible}$. To achieve this, we develop a comprehensive framework encompassing a wide range of lepton-flavor violating and conserving transformations within the Standard Model, in addition to various effective field theories. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of various experimental and theoretical constraints on the available operators, considering existing experimental data, as well as predicted outcomes for upcoming experiments such as the Belle II. Furthermore, we examine the distinct signatures of neutrino and dark energy sector contributions at the Belle II, particularly focusing on neutrino, dark energy, and semi-anonymous invisible decays, as well as considering contributions from various effective field theories. Lastly, we discuss the distinct signatures of neutrino and dark energy sector contributions at the LHC, specifically focusing on neutrino, dark energy, and semi-anonymous invisible decays, as well as considering contributions from various effective field theories.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis.

This study introduces the multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) framework, which adapts the singular spectrum analysis (SSA) method for discovering patterns in multivariate time series data constructed from multiple functional time series. The development of MFSSA enables researchers to analyze multivariate functional time series data, potentially identifying pattern components and estimating reconstruction errors. The efficacy of MFSSA is demonstrated through applications involving large datasets, including regional temperature variations across the United States and integrated electrical brain signal data. The performance of MFSSA is compared to the multivariate functional extension of SSA (MFESSA), with variations depending on the dimensional domain in question. The comparative assessment highlights the advantages and limitations of each approach. The MFSSA R package, available on CRAN, provides users with access to the MFSSA function for downloading dataset extras and viewing the code. The package also includes additional functions derived from the multivariate functional time series analysis framework.

Deep learning-based automated driving emergency assistance systems and self-driving vehicles rely heavily on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to predict and respond to certain traffic situations known as 'events'. However, recent research revealed a potentially dangerous phenomenon called 'overstimulation' or'stimulation explosion', where these neural networks are excessively activated by combining two events that the network has previously learned separately. In order to tackle this critical issue, this paper delves into the underlying causes of overstimulation, attributing it to two contributors: overresponse to individual events and the instability of the network's event representations. In addition, we introduce a mathematical concept to measure overstimulation and propose a novel evaluation metric that simulates human perception. To address this issue, the paper presents two defense strategies: (1) a data augmentation technique called 'composite event clipping' that prevents the network from focusing on specific aspects of an event, and (2) an ensemble-based approach that leverages multiple representations of the same event to encourage the network to pay attention to general features rather than unique ones. Experimental results demonstrate that these proposed defenses are capable of reducing overstimulation in multiple scenarios.

This study examines a one-dimensional random walk that continues until a stopping time $T$ is reached, where the probability measure is re-normalized by the length $\tau$ of the walk. The main goal is to establish an inequality that provides an upper bound on the second moment of $\tau$, along with an identity that holds under specific conditions and provides a lower bound on the first moment of $\tau$. These results can be applied to demonstrate the convergence in probability of the normalized last hitting place probability and derive an explicit expression for the second moment of the last exit time from a finite interval.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is undergoing a transformation to meet new safety standards, which will result in a significant modification to its plasma chamber. A new plasma source, designed for helicon wave production, has been installed as part of these changes. To ensure accuracy, computer simulations were used to model the new plasma source, and their results were compared with actual measurements taken during recent experiments. Although some discrepancies were found, they were ultimately confirmed to be the result of measurement errors, and good agreement was found between the simulations and a previous study. The validated simulations can now be used to gain a deeper understanding of the plasma source's operation and will be instrumental in identifying areas that could benefit from improvement, such as the plasma source's narrow current distribution.

This research paper presents a mathematical model aimed at addressing the challenges facing microbial biopesticide implementation. The model identifies two rival methods, chemical pesticides and resistance microorganisms, which hinder the biopesticide's effectiveness. The model consists of a system of ordinary differential equations representing the dynamics of susceptible and resistant host populations as well as the biopesticide population. The model's stability at an equilibrium point, where the biopesticide population is sufficiently high to manage the infection, is the primary focus of this study. Additionally, the research investigates the biopesticide's potential to regulate the host population through dietary supplementation. A numerical study is also included to illustrate the impact of increased consumption on the biopesticide's efficacy.

In precision medicine, identifying cancer cells through image analysis is a crucial step in treating patients and determining the best course of treatment.  However, accurately detecting these cells is extremely difficult and there is a lot of interest in using artificial intelligence methods to automate this process.  By improving detection of these cells, the effectiveness of treatments can also be assessed more accurately.  To address this challenge, a new approach called W-Net has been developed, an automated system that uses two stages to better capture the details of these cells.  First, it uses a preliminary stage to locate potential cells and then uses the positions of these cells to guide a second stage that refines the capture of these cells.  By using this two-stage approach, W-Net has shown a greater ability to detect these cells more accurately than existing methods.  The team behind this innovation has also demonstrated its ability to capture the intricate details of these cells by including a third stage that uses the outputs of the two previous stages.  By testing this approach on a large dataset of images, the team found that W-Net outperformed existing methods, particularly in capturing the nuclei of these cells, a critical component of these cells.  By comparing the results of this approach with that of an existing method, particularly in capturing the shapes and orientation of these cells, the team found that W-Net performed similarly to this method, but still required optimization, a critical aspect, and that there was still a significant disparity between the performance of this

Let's consider a field of characteristic not two and label it as $k$. Additionally, let's denote an infinite number of prime numbers greater than the characteristic of $k$ as $\{p_n\}$. The parameter $p$ will represent a finite subset of $\{p_n\}$. 

This paper proves a converse theorem for specific subgroups of $G_{\mathfrak{p}}$, which are derived from the absolute Galois group of $k$ and where $\mathfrak{p}$ represents a finite subset of $\{p_n\}$. The subgroups in question are the kernel of the reduction map from $G_{\mathfrak{p}}$ to the product of the reduction maps to the absolute Galois groups of the residue fields, with the property that the reduction map is finite and surjective for an infinite number of prime numbers in $\{p_n\}$. 

The proof relies on an earlier strategy, specifically the approach described in the paper 'The regional converse theorem for GL_n in positive characteristic', to which this paper is an extension. Consequently, the results from the paper 'The regional converse theorem for GL_n in positive characteristic' become special cases of the results derived here.

A graph G is considered to have an detectable hamiltonian property if both G and its line graph G^1 can exhibit a hamiltonian path. This study aims to broaden this concept by introducing the idea of an graph G having an n-th order detectable hamiltonian property, which is defined as both G and its n-th iterated line graph G^n possessing a hamiltonian path. This study also introduces the hamiltonian route index of a graph, which is the smallest number n required for its line graph, IN(n), to possess a hamiltonian path.

Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19.  Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation which can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection.  Research into pyroptosis's role in COVID-19 progression is ongoing, but there's a recognized need to investigate potential anti-inflammatory treatments.  This study develops a solitary-cell model that captures the processes of SARS-CoV-2 infection, NLRP3 inflammasome formation, and pyroptotic cell death, including the effects of inflammation on cell death.  The model is then used to explore the dynamics of pyroptosis in COVID-19 and the benefits of suppressing the NLRP3 inflammasome to prevent cell death.

External influences affecting states and rewarding behavior in reinforcement learning can hinder training efficiency and compromise solution stability. This issue is addressed by developing a framework that automatically identifies and eliminates such extrinsic state variables and reward signals, enabling a reduced and isolated learning environment. The framework's effectiveness is showcased through the optimization of control policies achieved by removing physically irrelevant sensor readings from a robotic simulation, as well as the discovery of uncorrelated reward pathways in a variety of multi-task reinforcement learning scenarios.

A blockchain-based smart contract on Tezos, specifically on the Haskell implementation called HELM, is validated using a vendor-neutral inspection method based on refinement types. This approach, developed by the HELM project, offers a independent and language-agnostic verification procedure. As a result, the project has yielded a versatile refinement type system, called hlm2tex, capable of translating refinement types into the Michelson programming language used for Tezos smart contracts. This translation has been fully implemented in a validation tool called hlm2tex, which provides users with the capability to verify Tezos smart contracts written in HELM through type checking, as well as the ability to utilize external libraries and tools. Additionally, the project has introduced innovative features such as array and option refinement types, appraisals, and do-notation for simplifying the expression of refinements. The development of hlm2tex offers a promising pathway for the integration of refinement types and type checking in blockchain-based smart contracts.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite deviations from traditional neural network designs. To address this disparity, we developed a non-neural network approach using matched filtering, demonstrating equivalent functionally equivalent results to GCNNs in various applications, including image feature extraction and classification, and molecular property prediction. By providing a theoretical filter design framework, we showcase its generality across distinct use cases and provide a more intuitive understanding of GCNN operations.

In three-dimensional space, gravity can be represented using a Chern-Simons action for a connection that includes a hairy black hole or soliton. This action also accommodates a scalar field with a conserved charge, which in turn generates an effect on the space-time geometry. The presence of a non-zero scalar field causes a shift in the black hole or soliton mass, which in turn affects the conserved charge. The relationship between these two quantities remains unchanged, allowing for the definition of an effective mass, which is conserved in both cases. The combination of Chern-Simons gravity and a scalar field leads to the formation of solitons with negative mass and black holes with masses proportional to the charge, which vary depending on the gauge force employed. The behavior of these solutions holds consistent across various gauge forces, as demonstrated through the use of an electric potential that pinches the space-time at the object's core, differentiating it from the flat space outside. The addition of a Chern-Simons term for a gauge force results in an adjustment to the soliton or black hole mass, which in turn affects the charge conservation, now based on the potential at the object's core rather than the total charge. The adoption of a specific gauge force causes the charge to become conserved, allowing for the coexistence of a non-zero chemical potential and a non-trivial configuration of the scalar field. We've established an analogy between the M-balls process and a specific configuration of interacting particles undergoing a reversible inclusion-exclusion process. This analogy reveals a uniquely configured membrane system that maintains non-reversible symmetry through the exclusion of specific particles. Additionally, our findings demonstrate that at equilibrium, the M-balls process is equivalent to a particular Ising model with long-range interactions. Furthermore, we've identified a distinct critical point arising from the non-reversible feature of the inclusion-exclusion process, which separates two regimes related to the exclusion process: one corresponds to the coexistence of two distinct species within the M-balls process, while the other represents a random placement of particles within the M-balls process.

Precise location estimation in ultrasound elastography, particularly lateral displacement, is critical for diagnosing medical conditions, but current methods fall short due to limited spatial sampling and synthetic array limitations. To overcome these challenges, we present a Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture (VOSA) technique, combining the advantages of focused and plane wave ultrasound to improve location estimation precision. By leveraging the focused wave's high lateral resolution and the plane wave's uniform coverage, VOSA enables accurate detection of tissue displacements, even in soft tissue environments. Numerical analysis and experimental results demonstrate that VOSA outperforms existing methods, providing a more precise and robust solution for diagnosing medical conditions using ultrasound elastography.

Students learn programming concepts best through explicit connections between theoretical explanations and hands-on experiences, including both algorithmic descriptions and practical coding exercises. To strengthen these connections, we introduce a new approach to teaching programming concepts using "rational pseudocode," a graphical representation of fundamental principles. This approach focuses on abstracting technology details to highlight essential computational concepts. We've applied this method to create a comprehensive set of educational materials covering basic data structures and algorithms. These resources incorporate rational pseudocodes alongside step-by-step breakdowns of algorithm implementations in multiple programming languages. We've gathered empirical evidence to support the effectiveness of this method in improving student understanding of programming concepts through examples of student outcomes and instructor feedback. We believe our approach can be valuable for any educational initiative aiming to teach fundamental programming concepts.

This study aims to establish various Ramsey properties within the Boolean algebras generated by a family of posets with V-shapes, specifically focusing on posets whose peaks consist of a single element and whose chains have a minimum length of two. We prove a number of V-shape Theorems to achieve this goal, leveraging these results to derive corollaries on the V-shape Ramsey properties of finite lattices and the infinite lattice obtained by combining multiple V-shapes.

In the context of high-dimensional data, our study focuses on an adapted version of the dynamic $k$-means clustering problem, where we're working with a continuous stream of points with unknown or fixed labels. Our primary concern is minimizing the storage required to hold the centroid representatives of the clusters. We've developed a simplified storage approach that only holds the median of the current point's neighbors among the previous data set, and this has very brief overhead compared to the overall data size. Our main achievement is ensuring that with a fixed proportion of stored centroid representatives, our algorithm can recover the existing clusters and assign each new point to a cluster with a probability of at least $1-e^{-\Omega(d\epsilon^2)}$ if the data points have a fixed mean distance from each other and the clustering structure is robust enough. Additionally, we've established an lower bound to show that the storage requirement for an almost optimal dynamic $k$-means clustering algorithm increases with the number of data dimensions.

We're investigating a series of hierarchical games where a single agile predator navigates a random environment to catch multiple evaders. The evaders are indistinguishable and possess equal capabilities. We've established a method for determining the optimal cooperative behavior among the evaders and have discovered that it yields a 1.5 times improvement in expected capture time compared to a single evader. Furthermore, our findings reveal that collaborative effort can lead to capture avoidance up to 75% of the time. The study also explores the dynamics of uncooperative behavior among the evaders, which results in the emergence of dominant and submissive roles in the pursuit-evasion game.

We're exploring the concept of circular and nontransitive probabilities in an objective probability measure. This involves examining a set of probabilities that form a cyclic pattern under the application of a given function. Our research also delves into the requirements for a set of numbers to maintain nontransitive properties under specific functions. We've discovered limitations on nontransitive probabilities within standard scales, finding that only fractions less than one can maintain this property. However, we've found that certain transformations can preserve nontransitive probabilities. We've developed methods for determining the implications of these transformations on nontransitive probabilities. Our work on circular probabilities reveals that only the probabilities at the edges of a triangle can contribute to a nontransitive probability triplet. We've found that the simplest way to create a nontransitive probability triplet is by using the probabilities of different outcomes from different trials of a single random process. We've established that this type of triplet will always exhibit both nontransitive and circular properties. Our work has implications for the design of systems that exhibit nontransitive or circular behavior in scenarios involving uncertainty or randomness.

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A particular method known as the unsupervised cycleGAN approach has shown great promise, but currently available implementations fail to achieve balanced improvement in both CT image denoising and tissue density preservation. To address this limitation, we introduce the AdaIN-Switchable cycleGAN, which combines an attention mechanism with a cycleGAN framework to enable adaptive learning of noise patterns and density preservation. By switching the direction of mapping functions, our model can learn from low-dose to regular-dose CT images while rejecting unnecessary information, and from regular-dose to low-dose CT images while retaining important tissue density. The experimental results, validated by both quantitative metrics and clinical ratings, demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing cycleGAN implementations and achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art denoising networks while maintaining efficiency and simplicity.

Recent successes in dialogue comprehension tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialogues as positive examples, forcing unrelated dialogues together. To address this issue, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. It combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training to learn dialogue representations from labeled and unlabeled dialogues. To begin with, it proposes a general semantic tree structure (STS) that unifies diverse annotation formats, making use of all labeled data's rich structural information. Next, it suggests a novel multi-view score function to focus on task-relevant content and incorporate the STS. To supplement labeled data, it incorporates an encoding process for unlabeled dialogues, using these representations as negative examples along with pseudo annotations during training. Experimental results show SPACE-2 achieves notable improvements over baselines in convergence speed and performance on diverse dialogue comprehension tasks.
This research aims to investigate an ideal fluid spacetime's conformal Ricci-Yamabe soliton and derive its associated metric and energy distribution within a geometric framework.

To study the rotational characteristics of distorted halo nuclei, we employed the angular momentum projection method onto total ground state wavefunctions.  Using the long-range monopole and spin-dipole responses as indicators, we investigated shape uncoupling in 43Ca and 45Ar.  Our findings suggest that for 43Ca, the ground state is primarily an s-wave with a distorted halo structure, and little shape uncoupling is observed.  In contrast, 45Ar exhibits significant shape uncoupling due to its ground state being composed of both s and d-wave components, resulting from the interaction between its halo and cluster structures.

A common video super-resolution technique uses optical flow to predict missing frames, but this can lead to estimation difficulties due to the presence of motion, noise, and real-world occlusions, especially when training with just 100 frames. We enhance this method by dividing the video into segments and using two separate models for frame prediction: one that handles adjacent frames with motion estimation, and another for long-term propagation. To improve alignment, we modify the motion estimation model to use feature-based alignment, using both horizontal and vertical features to predict vertical and horizontal shifts. This is done by adding two auxiliary branches to the prediction network, allowing it to learn shift offsets directly from features. We apply this approach to video super-resolution, and our implementation is BasicVSR++, in which the modified prediction network is pre-trained and then fine-tuned for specific datasets. Our method achieves better performance and lower mean squared error when compared to other video super-resolution techniques, particularly in the OMNET dataset, according to four objective evaluation metrics, and also produces higher visual quality, as shown in user studies.

This study proposes an efficient method for estimating vector boson distributions in high-energy muon collisions using a new variable based on the Collins-Aizenman theorem. By simplifying the complex data analysis, this method significantly reduces theoretical uncertainties and experimental errors associated with jet resummation, leading to more accurate predictions of heavy quark distributions. Our research indicates that the new estimation technique yields highly reliable results for W and Z boson production, inviting further exploration of this method in other processes.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, models are often shared across tasks to induce a beneficial transfer of knowledge. However, when the tasks have dissimilar goals, this sharing can lead to negative effects due to goal conflicts. To address this issue, we propose a new method of sharing that uses modular systems. By isolating key features from a shared representation, our approach prevents negative interactions between tasks. We demonstrate theoretically and practically that this method avoids the detrimental interference experienced in non-modular multi-task reinforcement learning. Furthermore, we show through a set of experiments that our approach outperforms the standard multi-task method even when the tasks share a significant amount of goal-related information.

This study provides a precise estimate for the gradient of the solution's approximation in the porous medium type equation and the rapid diffusion type equation on a noncompact manifold with a compact boundary. The key challenge here is that the given space is not compact, which necessitates establishing boundedness for the solution's approximation and its gradient. The obtained estimate for the gradient's approximation holds under the assumption $\frac{\mu}{\lambda} - \frac{n}{2} > 1$, where $\mu$ and $\lambda$ denote the exponent and $n$ represents the dimension of the manifold respectively. The method of fractional step on the whole space is adapted and modified for the boundary case, which yields the desired estimate. Furthermore, this estimate leads to the convergence proof of the discrete approximation method.

In 1934, Kurt Godel and Alonzo Church corresponded, with Church informing Godel about his recent work involving the incompleteness theorem and the development of a formal system whose validity could not be determined within the system itself.  However, it is widely acknowledged that Church's information was already known to Godel in advance of their published conversation.  This paper explores the underlying circumstances of this event, including the role of Stephen Kleene and the influence of Gödel's 1930 Princeton lecture.  Additionally, the paper examines the subsequent reactions of Max Tarski, Rudolf Carnap, and Elliott Turrell (J.B. Rosser), among others, and discusses the broader implications of Gödel's discovery for the field of mathematical logic.

This paper formulates three-sphere theorems for functions solving a complex analytic problem, specifically the Dirac equation, within the framework of Clifford analysis. To establish these results, a suitable factorization of the inhomogeneous equation is needed, along with a suitable adaptation of the Cauchy-Kovrijkina's Integral Formula. Consequently, this formulation enables the derivation of conclusions analogous to those proven in traditional complex analysis, including the representation of solutions via power series and a version of the three-sphere theorem.

When conducting surveys, it is common to use a geographically balanced sampling frame to ensure diversity of responses. This paper proposes an innovative method of sequentially selecting balanced samples. Firstly, an initial sample is chosen randomly from a normal distribution. This sample is then used to determine specific coordinates for inclusion in the next phase of selection. The process continues until a final sample size is achieved. This method of geographically balanced sampling is compared to traditional methods using simulated data and real-world examples. The results show that sequential sampling maintains a high level of balance while reducing the time and effort required.

To facilitate robotic grasping and manipulation, having control over the camera perspective is crucial. This study proposes a novel method to automatically regulate the eye-in-hand camera position solely with visual information. We developed and tested this approach using a Kuka robot and a Realsense camera in real-world settings, incorporating both simulated and real-world environments. The method outperformed human performance in a simulation game, Mario, and successfully adapted to changes in lighting conditions and the color and texture of objects in a test room.

In scenarios like experimental measurements or image analysis, identifying the underlying parameters that generate data is a critical task. When data is contaminated with noise, finding the exact parameters is impossible, but estimating the posterior distribution of those parameters is feasible. To tackle this challenge, we develop a method based on a regularization technique for conditional generators, allowing them to learn an efficient representation of the data that minimizes the discrepancy between the generated and actual data, while also capturing the biases of the data as indicated by the prior. This approach yields a probabilistic model, represented by the conditioned generator's output being uniformly distributed, which facilitates measuring the discrepancy between the data and the model's predictions. We incorporate two regularization techniques: one that eliminates unnecessary dimensions of the data and penalizes the complexity of the generator, and another that uses dropout regulation to account for the instability of the training process. We also explore alternative methods for measuring the discrepancy, including maximum likelihood estimation. Our proposed method surpasses the performance of existing techniques, such as the inverse problem solution method, in multiple test cases.

This study examines the concept of invariant surfaces in dynamical systems from a mathematical perspective, specifically focusing on their properties and the conditions required. Surface invariance in a dynamical system is determined by the equation $N'(x) = \lambda N(x)$, where $N(x)$ represents the mapping of $x$ onto the surface and $\lambda$ defines the eigenvalue. Without loss of generality, the case where $\lambda = 0$ is considered, and the condition for a surface to remain invariant is expressed as the equation $\frac{d}{dx}(\lambda N(x)) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} J N(x) = 0$. A specific mapping $N(x)$ is introduced, and the existence of surfaces in two-dimensional and three-dimensional dynamical systems is demonstrated through numerical examples. Furthermore, the paper investigates conditions under which surfaces cannot exist, leading to the conclusion that in a nonlinear system with a linear mapping, surfaces cannot exist if the matrix of derivatives is not identically zero.

Due to the high path loss of Terahertz communications, using very short transmission distances with the aid of relay nodes is a common practice. This study proposes utilizing learning techniques to optimize the process of beam training in these multi-hop communications, as even reducing the number of required transmissions significantly improves performance. To achieve this, an agent learns from its environment by controlling the formation of the main and relay antennas' beams in order to maximize the overall data transfer rate. This framework is then enhanced by implementing a deep reinforcement learning approach with a complex state space, yielding positive results.

The line of sight to high-luminosity pulsars offers a unique chance to explore the interstellar medium in the line's narrow zone. By examining scintillation patterns of the bright pulsar B1133+16, researchers discovered distinct plasma regions along its line of sight. A statistical analysis of the data allowed researchers to infer the presence of two separate regions, one with smaller scale sizes than the other, indicating varying levels of turbulence. The findings suggest that the interstellar medium in the Perseus arm may contain a turbulent region with significant scale sizes, potentially influencing the distribution of matter and energy in the region.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for speech and music. To overcome this challenge, we incorporated a decomposed approach, separating the generation process into two stages based on the quasi-periodic nature of audio waveforms. In the first stage, a coarse signal is produced at a higher sampling rate, and in the second stage, a fine signal is generated at the original sampling rate through up-sampling and non-linearity. To facilitate periodical signal modeling, we included a memory mechanism and a hypernetwork for adaptive resampling, and incorporated a decomposed technique for network training. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our proposed model over the original WaveNet through various evaluation metrics, including higher F-score values and more accurate mel cepstral distance metrics. Furthermore, our model excels in harmonic synthesis tasks in both music and speech contexts.

This research presents a novel web-based tool, dubbed MADARi, which tackles both Arabic morphological annotation and text spelling correction simultaneously. In line with traditional morphological analysis methods for Arabic, MADARi's core aim is to identify the root and pattern of words, a task made intricate due to the language's agglutinative nature and vast, unresolved issues in Arabic NLP. To effectively handle these challenges, the development of MADARi involved several computational techniques, including a unique, hybrid approach to spell checking, combined with a custom, rule-based morphological analyzer. Furthermore, the platform features a user-friendly interface and a range of user support tools. In contrast to existing Arabic morphological analyzers, MADARi's key differentiator is its ability to recognize unstandardized spellings, achieved through the incorporation of Arabic standard spellings and a lemmatizer. Additionally, the platform has shown promising results in evaluation tests, including a 80% success rate in morphological analysis and a 90% accuracy rate in spell checking.

Planets within the habitable zone of a star may still lack conditions for life if their atmosphere is overwhelmed by photosynthetic biomass sealing off surface areas from the star's rays. Even if habitable to current standards, low-level starlight might not trigger sufficient molecular oxygen buildup. Alternatively, high stellar energies could extinguish all life forms before oxygen can accumulate, regardless of the planet's distance from the star. 

Analyzing various scenarios involving gas-filled habitable worlds through chemical kinetics and radiative transfer, our research reveals the complex interplay between exotic and organic substances in response to different stellar radiations. Various photochemical reactions lead to an expanded gas spectrum, often displaying distinct features when comparing various exoplanets. 

In contrast to existing approaches that treat habitable planets as a single entity, this study uses a sophisticated model to study specific planets, incorporating their unique atmospheric composition and surrounding environmental factors. This involves simulations of various stellar types, atmospheric pressures, and molecular mixing ratios.

The interactions between organic and gas molecules respond uniquely to changes in solar energy, resulting in altered spectral patterns that distinguish the photochemistry of distinct planets. This difference highlights the importance of selecting target exoplanets based on their unique spectral patterns when using spectroscopy to study their bio-signatures.

Ultimately, identifying the source of observed spectral patterns as living organisms or inanimate matter requires an understanding of the photochemical processes that shape the atmosphere of gas-filled planets. This study demonstrates the potential for combining data on exoplanet atmospheres

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves incorporating ohmic damping into tunneling spectroscopy using resistive electrodes. Introducing a thermal broadening factor that is proportional to the temperature and electrode resistance, this technique makes the Majorana peak more distinct by changing the shape of the peak in response to varying temperature and electrode resistance. While remaining unaffected by gate voltage and superconducting gap, the thermal broadening factor unique to the Majorana peak allows for its identification, providing a solution to the differentiation problem despite it not being a peak per se.

The development of advanced materials in highway construction has outpaced the creation of corresponding maintenance technologies. To resolve this issue, we've introduced RoadAtlas, a pioneering system that utilizes cutting-edge technologies like computer vision and the Internet of Things. This system is designed to efficiently identify defects, repair areas, and track assets on highways, enabling more effective and data-driven maintenance operations.

The shadow bicategory is an advancement of the classic concept of shadows introduced by Goldstein in 1983, and it's achievable through the process of categorifying edges in a bicategorical surface, resulting in the bicategorical version of that surface. By applying the categorification method to all components of a bicategorical polygon, we derive the bicategorical polygon's structure, and it accordingly includes the bicategorical triangle's structure which relates the loop space of a point to the loop space of a line. Furthermore, this connection between the shadow bicategory and loop spaces provides the basis for establishing isomorphisms between specific loop spaces and the category of presheaves on the shadow bicategory.

Comparing localization performance in free field and enclosed settings is a common practice, however, research has shown that free field testing overestimates sound localization abilities when in enclosed environments. This study's aim is to create a more challenging free field test that accurately predicts localization performance in enclosed environments. A method was proposed which involves recording the test sounds' characteristics in both free field and enclosed settings, and utilizing these characteristics to model the test sounds' localization in free field. This model was utilized to identify the test sounds that pose a difficulty in localization in free field, but do not in enclosed settings. As a result, a new set of test sounds was created which are poorly localized in free field but highly localized in enclosed settings. It was discovered that these test sounds' poor localization in free field is primarily due to front-back confusion, and that they are more susceptible to external noise. Furthermore, it was found that the test sounds that are difficult to localize in both free field and enclosed settings tend to have low spectral contrast.

Machine learning models are typically positioned in a Euclidean space to apply distance-based techniques such as k-means and graph neural networks (GNNs) using Euclidean distance to predict node classifications. However, this approach contradicts Einstein's theory of relativity, which states that space-time is curved and has inherent directions. Consequently, using the correct metric, namely the Lorentzian metric, can lead to more accurate predictions. We introduce a novel non-Euclidean GNN framework based on the Lorentzian metric, which enables the flexible representation of nodes in a hyperbolic space. By leveraging this metric, our model can efficiently learn node embeddings by manipulating the metric's inherent directions and producing more coherent hyperbolic representations. The proposed model exhibits superior performance compared to existing methods in benchmark experiments, and our analysis of hyperbolic representation learning has insightful findings on the detection of drifts in data distributions.

This research paper delves into the 'inverse problem' of determining a source region's acoustic properties within a confined space, given the acoustic field outside the source region. By assuming the source region maintains constant temperature and fluid properties, we use the boundary acoustic field to solve for the corresponding boundary values, effectively reversing the standard heat equation problem. Numerical solutions are derived using a finite element method for both linear and nonlinear source regions, with varying levels of complexity. The resulting algorithm is tested against experimental data, demonstrating its capability to recover source region properties. Additionally, the paper explores the possibility of recovering source region geometry through the inversion of a structural acoustic problem, where the source region is bounded by an elastic structure whose vibrations generate the acoustic field.

Optomechanical interactions offer a promising means to study quantum mechanics within a classical framework. A system consisting of a cavity filled with a nonlinear medium and linked to a heat reservoir through a mechanical element can facilitate this investigation. We examine the steady-state situation where an optical signal is transmitted through the system while being driven by an electrical heat source. Analysis reveals two regimes: in one, driven by thermal diffusion, correlated light is produced; in another, optical quantum states can be created through a quantum feedback process. Notably, this latter process can achieve a higher success probability than a direct method of state preparation.

We examine an expansion of modal $\mu$-calculus, specifically considering its application to systems consisting of multiple agents represented as finite graphs, $G_A$. Our investigation focuses on two variants: the basic $\mu$-calculus and the twisted $\mu$-calculus. These variants correspond to restricting and relaxing symmetry in the application of modal $\mu$-calculi to these systems respectively. Our analysis yields insights into the computational complexity of model checking and the verification of modal $\mu$-calculi in this setting, with outcomes dependent on whether the systems in question allow for parallel connections between their components. Our research also explores the relationship between these connections and the symmetry present in the systems. Additionally, we establish the inherent complexity of model checking in this context, showing it to be NP-complete for both parallel and nonparallel configurations. Our findings also indicate that in the absence of twisted branching, model checking can be accomplished efficiently. Moreover, we establish the equivalence between the basic and the twisted mu-calculus, as well as the equivalence between their closed fragments. Our investigation also compares the complexity of verifying vectorial $\mu$-calculi with that of scalar $\mu$-calculi, showing that the addition of vectorial operators does not enhance the computational complexity of model checking.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We demonstrate that our model
and the Tsallis model share identical parameter interrelations, and our model's
implications yield relevant insights. However, the Tsallis model's conclusions are
limiting in their scope. Moreover, we suggest a new methodology for testing the
Tsallis model.

We present a simplified harmonic gauge, known as the de Donder gauge, in the context of Einstein's general relativity. By simplifying the complex gauge conditions, we establish that the de Donder gauge can be defined by a single condition derived directly from the harmonic gauge. We then explore the implications of using this simplified gauge in the development of Einstein's general relativity, discussing the necessity of specific metric and Ricci tensor components in order to satisfy the de Donder gauge condition.

A signed graph is created by adding a polarity to the edges of an existing graph, and this concept of signed graphs has been extended to various other areas such as switching graphs and orientable graphs. A specific type of graph, known as an orientable graph, requires that the edges be arranged in a specific way to allow a path to exist between two nodes. Orientable graphs have a more general form known as Extended Double Covers (EDCs). EDCs were initially defined through a specific graph construction process, but a new definition has been proposed based solely on the properties of the graph itself. This new definition of an EDC has been shown to be an all-or-nothing condition, but the exact reasons for this are still unclear. On the other hand, a condition that a graph meet the criteria of being an EDC can be checked in a finite number of steps, but the problem of determining whether a given graph is an EDC remains unsolvable. When the process of constructing an EDC is repeated with smaller instances of the same graph, the resulting graph will contain a specific type of structure known as a homomorphism limit. However, when the process is applied to some specific types of graphs, such as cycles and trees, the resulting graph will contain a loop, which goes against its original intent.
